strengths: Well-motivated problem: Compelling visual evidence (Figure 1) demonstrating that existing LSNM methods fail under skewed noise, showing residual dependence in the true causal direction

Methodologically sound approach: Natural extension of LSNMs from Gaussian to skew-normal noise with backward compatibility; proper use of B-splines and principled ECM adaptation for parameter estimation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Novel synthetic datasets with three skewness levels, 11 baselines, ablation studies showing ECM necessity (28-34% improvements on LSs-IT), and both synthetic and established benchmarks
Exceptional performance on skewed noise: SKEWD-LL achieves 100% accuracy across all synthetic skewed-noise datasets while competitors degrade significantly (ROCHE: 81%, QCCD: 11% on LSs(1.750))
Strong reproducibility and presentation: Publicly available code promised, detailed hyperparameter specifications, thorough appendices, informative visualizations
weaknesses: Severely restricted scope: Limited to bivariate causal discovery, which is a significant limitation for a top venue; multivariate extension essential for real-world applicability

Computational complexity not addressed: Multi-stage optimization (Bayesian optimization → CMA-ES → ECM) lacks runtime comparisons with baselines; no scalability analysis provided; practical feasibility unclear

Incremental methodological novelty: Primary components (skew-normal distribution, B-splines, ECM) are well-established; main contribution is combining existing techniques for LSNMs, which feels somewhat incremental

Bounded skewness limitation: Skew-normal restricted to |γ₁| ≈ 0.9953, while many real distributions (e.g., exponential with γ₁=2) exceed this bound; limited applicability to heavily skewed real-world data

Modest improvements on real benchmarks: ROCHE outperforms SKEWD-LL on established benchmarks (87.69% vs 77.43%); SKEWD-IT achieves only 2.67% improvement, raising questions about practical significance

Experimental design concerns: Synthetic data generation follows existing baselines' schemes (potential bias); IGCI-G's perfect accuracy despite being 'highly misspecified' suggests dataset bias; limited real-world validation (only 99 Tübingen pairs)

Insufficient justification of assumptions: Likelihood scoring assumes Gaussian marginals without empirical verification; B-spline knot counts (q=14, p=7) appear arbitrary; bounds on λ and ρ lack principled justification
Missing statistical rigor: No significance tests between methods despite overlapping confidence intervals; no analysis of distributional assumptions' validity in practice
Limited real-world applicability: No experiments on domains with known skewed noise (e.g., economic, environmental data); identifiability assertions not explicitly verified for skew-normal case

strengths: Clear problem motivation with effective visual demonstration (Figure 1) of how Gaussian assumptions fail under skewed noise
Technically sound mathematical framework that properly extends existing identifiability results to skew-normal LSNMs
Comprehensive experimental design including novel synthetic datasets at varying skewness levels and 13 established benchmarks
Excellent empirical performance on purpose-built skew-noise datasets (100% accuracy with SKEWD-LL)
Convincing ablation study (Tables 2-3) demonstrating necessity of ECM refinement with improvements up to 34%
Dual inference strategies (likelihood and independence testing) provide flexibility
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: restriction to bivariate causal discovery is inadequate for ICML; multivariate extension relegated to future work despite being essential for real-world applicability
Incremental methodological novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (skew-normal distributions from Azzalini 1985 and ECM algorithms from Ferreira et al. 2023) without fundamental innovation

Experimental setup concerns: novel datasets are explicitly constructed with skew-normal noise, creating circular advantage for SKEWD-LL; IGCI-G's unexplained near-perfect performance suggests potential dataset artifacts
Mixed benchmark results: on established datasets (Table 1), SKEWD-IT ranks 2nd with 85.02% versus ROCHE's 87.69% (2.67% gap with no significance testing), and SKEWD-LL ranks 3rd at 77.43%
Restrictive noise model: skew-normal skewness bounded at γ₁ ≈ 0.9953 cannot handle γ₁ = 1.750 datasets; lacks capability for heavy-tailed distributions critical in many domains
Absent computational cost analysis: Algorithm 1's nested optimization (Bayesian optimization → CMA-ES → ECM) appears expensive but runtime comparisons, scalability, and complexity not addressed
Incomplete identifiability analysis: applicability of Theorem 1 to skew-normal LSNMs only briefly discussed; twice-differentiability requirement not rigorously verified
Limited statistical rigor: no hypothesis tests on benchmark results; unclear whether 2.67% difference with ROCHE is significant; modest benchmark set (13 datasets)
Weak treatment of fundamental limitations: necessary extensions (heavy tails, non-Gaussian marginals) dismissed as 'future work' rather than being addressed
Insufficient failure mode analysis: no deep investigation of when SKEWD-IT underperforms SKEWD-LL by 14% (86% vs 100% on LSs dataset) or systematic characterization of failure cases

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Figure 1 compellingly demonstrates how assuming symmetric noise in the presence of skewed noise leads to incorrect causal inference—a genuine limitation of existing LSNM methods.

Sound technical approach: Skew-normal distribution naturally generalizes normal (λ=0 case); identifiability preserved; maximum likelihood framework with penalized likelihood is principled; ablation studies convincingly justify ECM refinement.

Thorough experimental evaluation: Novel synthetic datasets with controlled skewness levels; comprehensive comparison against 10 baselines across 19 datasets; both accuracy and AUDRC metrics; perfect performance on skewed-noise benchmarks while remaining competitive on established datasets.

Strong empirical results on target domain: SKEWD-LL achieves 100% accuracy across all skewed noise datasets; SKEWD-IT maintains competitive performance (85.02% vs ROCHE 87.69%) on established benchmarks.
Reproducibility: Code to be released publicly; detailed hyperparameters and implementation details in appendices; clear algorithmic descriptions enabling verification.
Clear presentation: Well-organized with effective visualizations, accessible technical content, and honest limitations discussion appropriate for the venue.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Skew-normal distribution is established (Azzalini 1985), ECM algorithm substantially adapted from prior work (Ferreira et al. 2023). Contribution primarily combines existing techniques rather than introducing new methods or theory, warranting close scrutiny of empirical validation.

Restrictive bivariate scope: Method only distinguishes X→Y vs Y←X; cannot learn full causal structures. Multivariate extension relegated to future work, significantly limiting practical applicability for real-world causal discovery problems.

Identifiability under skewness not rigorously analyzed: Relies on Immer et al. (2023) without verifying differentiability conditions for skew-normal LSNMs. Skew-normal bounds |γ₁|<0.9953 but experiments include GNO with γ₁≈1.750, causing model misspecification. Lack of theoretical characterization when λ≠0.

Likelihood scoring assumptions inadequately validated: Assumes normal marginal distributions (Prop. 1 provides asymptotic justification only). No empirical validation that marginal normality holds on actual datasets or sensitivity analysis when marginals are skewed—violates core assumption.

Computational complexity uncharacterized: Multi-stage optimization (Bayesian opt → 8-fold CV → CMA-ES → ECM) appears expensive; no runtime comparisons with baselines; no scalability analysis; practical computational cost barrier unquantified for readers.

Limited real-world validation: Only 99/19 total datasets are real data (Tübingen benchmark); synthetic data generated with unspecified 'randomly sampled sigmoidal functions' potentially favoring method. No evaluation on documented skewed-noise domains (coastal flooding, rainfall) cited in motivation.

Independence testing details underexplored: HSIC test chosen without justification; robustness to test choice unexplored. Under model misspecification, even correct direction may show residual-cause dependence.

Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis absent: Many hyperparameters (q, p, α, κ, bounds on ρ, λ); limited sensitivity analysis; choices appear somewhat arbitrary. How robust is performance to these selections?

Missing comparison to related work: No comparison to Lin et al. (2024) on skewness-based causal discovery despite citation; fourth-moment methods (Cai et al. 2020) not compared despite addressing related heteroscedastic noise; ROCHE (t-distribution) could be more competitive if properly tuned.

Convergence and theoretical analysis gaps: No finite-sample convergence rates for parameter estimates or ECM algorithm; Tübingen pair 69 required iteration limit reduction (500 vs 5000), suggesting potential stability issues not discussed; no formal characterization of when SKEWD outperforms symmetric methods.

strengths: Identifies and clearly demonstrates a practical problem overlooked in existing literature—that standard LSNM methods assume symmetric noise distributions, which is violated in real-world domains
Comprehensive experimental validation including novel synthetic benchmarks with controlled skewness levels, 13 established benchmarks, multiple SOTA baselines, and thorough ablation studies
Two complementary inference variants (likelihood-based and independence-based) providing flexibility for different settings
Technically sound adaptation of ECM algorithms for GAM parameter estimation in the skew-normal setting
Honest discussion of method limitations including marginal Gaussianity assumptions, scalability constraints, and potential model misspecification
Novel contribution of benchmark datasets with varying skewness levels (γ₁ ∈ {-0.455, 0.985, 1.750}) useful for future research
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily applies existing techniques (skew-normal distributions, ECM algorithms, GAMs) to an existing model class rather than developing fundamentally new methods

Concerning empirical results: method underperforms SOTA on established benchmarks (Table 1, 85.02% vs. ROCHE's 87.69%), suggesting overspecialization to skewed noise problem with unclear practical benefit on realistic data

Complex three-step optimization (Bayesian optimization → CMA-ES → ECM) lacks full justification; unclear why simpler alternatives (e.g., direct ECM with cross-validation) are insufficient; no computational cost comparisons

Strong marginal Gaussianity assumption in likelihood scoring relies on asymptotic results; violations on finite samples acknowledged in appendix but not addressed; ablation shows KDE marginals significantly improve performance on non-Gaussian data

Multivariate extension (SKEWD-MV) is limited and ad-hoc: depends entirely on PC algorithm for MEC estimation, only evaluated on synthetic data (d≤10), acknowledged to have exponential scalability limitations, lacks real-world multivariate validation

Model misspecification concerns: skew-normal bounded to γ₁ ≈ 0.9953 but tests on GNO distributions with γ₁=1.750; GNO also exhibits different tail behavior and excess kurtosis; paper demonstrates robustness but doesn't characterize when such misspecification is acceptable
Identifiability analysis entirely relies on existing work without characterizing when skew-normal LSNMs specifically help or hurt identifiability beyond general LSNM results
Lack of real-world validation: no application to actual datasets with known skewed noise properties despite citing examples; only real data evaluation is on Tübingen bivariate pairs

IGCI-G anomaly unexplained: achieves comparable performance to SKEWD on skewed datasets (100%) despite being described as 'highly misspecified,' suggesting either incomplete analysis or baseline implementation issues

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly demonstrates via Figure 1 how symmetric noise assumptions lead to incorrect causal inference under skewness
Sound technical approach: carefully derived ECM algorithm with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Comprehensive experimental design: novel synthetic datasets with controlled skewness, 13 established benchmarks, ablation studies, and robustness checks
Strong performance on skewed synthetic data: achieves 100% accuracy on bivariate benchmarks with controlled skewness levels
Reasonable justification for skew-normal choice: discusses alternatives and articulates why skew-normal is preferable (unbounded support, generalizes Gaussian, sufficient flexibility)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing tools (skew-normal distributions from Azzalini 1985, ECM from Ferreira et al. 2023, standard causal discovery frameworks) without fundamental innovation

Suspiciously perfect synthetic results: 100% accuracy on 8/12 synthetic benchmarks suggests data generation may be overly favorable; GNO robustness tests (64-92% accuracy) indicate overfitting to skew-normal assumption
Weak performance on established benchmarks: SKEWD-IT achieves only 85.02% vs ROCHE's 87.69% on 13 real-world benchmarks (2.67% gap), undermining claims about practical importance of skewness

Restrictive assumptions limiting applicability: Gaussianity assumption for marginals (SKEWD-LL) causes substantial performance degradation per Appendix B.6; Gaussianity violations reduce accuracy by up to 22% on non-Gaussian benchmarks

Severe scalability limitations for multivariate case: only tested on d=6,10 with sparse graphs; SKEWD-MV-O oracle achieves SHD=0.14 vs SKEWD-MV's 2.27, indicating massive performance degradation when MEC is estimated; impractical for realistic problems

Computational complexity not addressed: three-stage optimization (Bayesian + CMA-ES + ECM) with cross-validation is expensive, but no runtime comparisons provided; special handling needed for large datasets (e.g., limiting ECM to 500 iterations for Tübingen pair 69)

Insufficient evidence for problem prevalence: single citation (Genton 2004) for claiming skewness is common in real data; t-distribution baseline (ROCHE) outperforms SKEWD on real benchmarks, suggesting skewness may not be dominant issue
Weak independence testing variant: SKEWD-IT is 2.67% below ROCHE; Table 3 shows 28-34% improvement from ECM refinement, indicating poor heuristic optimization and robustness concerns

No new theoretical contributions: relies entirely on Immer et al. (2023) and Strobl & Lasko (2023) for identifiability; Proposition 5.1 is straightforward; no characterization of when skew-normal is appropriate vs alternatives

Incomplete experimental comparisons: no comparison with Lin et al. (2024) skewness-based method despite being mentioned; CAREFL dismissed without thorough investigation; no comparison with skew-t despite discussion
Parameter restriction reduces applicability: λ ∈ [-25, 25] limits max skewness to 0.9887 vs 0.9953 theoretical max; GNO benchmarks exceed this range, but handled only via appendix ablation
Presentation issues: key results (mean accuracy 84.56%) relegated to appendix; paper is dense; Figure 1 duplicated; relationship between bivariate and multivariate extensions unclear

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical relevance (skewed noise in LSNMs) and compelling empirical demonstration (Figure 1) that existing methods fail
Principled choice of skew-normal distribution with thorough justification (Section 3.2) comparing alternatives and grounding in identifiability theory
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 19 datasets total (13 established + 6 novel skew-noise), multiple metrics (accuracy, AUDRC, SHD, SID), and ablation studies (ECM necessity, KDE margins)
Technically sound parameter estimation approach with clear ECM derivation, two-stage optimization strategy validated by ablation study (Table 3)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation details (Appendix B.1), explicit algorithms, hyperparameter specifications, and promise of code release
Honest treatment of limitations: discusses scalability constraints (Section 5.3), identifies when assumptions may fail, and investigates marginal density estimation robustness (Appendix B.6)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing skew-normal distribution (Azzalini 1985) to LSNMs with ECM algorithm adapted from Ferreira et al. (2023); no new theoretical results on identifiability under skewness

Gaussian marginal assumption for likelihood scoring (SKEWD-LL) significantly limits generality and is only justified asymptotically; KDE ablation (Appendix B.6) shows this assumption problematic on non-Gaussian benchmarks with no principled guidance on when to use which variant

Severe scalability limitations for multivariate extension (SKEWD-MV): only tested up to d=10, computational cost grows exponentially with undirected edges (2^υ-1 PCCs), and authors acknowledge suitability only for 'smaller-scale problems'

Reliance on PC algorithm for MEC estimation introduces fragility; no robustness analysis if PC fails or misspecifies MEC, and no performance analysis on realistic settings where oracle MEC unavailable

Mixed results on standard benchmarks: SKEWD-IT ranks 2nd at 85.02% vs. ROCHE 87.69% (Table 1), SKEWD-LL significantly worse at 77.43%; main strength limited to novel skewed-noise datasets with minimal real-world validation (only 99 Tübingen pairs)
Incomplete comparisons: Lin et al. (2024) addresses skewness-based causal discovery but is mentioned only in Related Work without empirical comparison; no comparison with CAREFL on main benchmarks

Parameter estimation complexity with three-stage optimization (Bayesian opt → CMA-ES → ECM) increases computational cost and fragility (e.g., Tübingen pair 69 limited to 500 ECM iterations); no convergence analysis or sensitivity study

Missing model diagnostics: no goodness-of-fit tests or guidance for practitioners to assess if skew-normal assumption is appropriate; unclear sensitivity when actual distribution deviates substantially from skew-normal
